title: Meta Will Build Its First AI Data Centre in India. Reliance Will Run It From Ambani's Jamnagar Complex.
excerpt: The 168-megawatt facility — powered by renewable energy, cooled by desalinated seawater — marks the deepest infrastructure bet any American tech giant has made in India. Delivery is expected within two years.
body:
Meta Platforms and Reliance Industries have signed what both companies are calling a landmark deal: a 168-megawatt, built-to-suit AI data centre in Jamnagar, Gujarat, that will serve as Meta's first dedicated AI computing facility in India.

The agreement, announced this week, puts Mark Zuckerberg's company inside Mukesh Ambani's flagship energy complex — a location chosen for its access to power, water, and Reliance Jio's fibre network. Reliance will design, build, and operate the facility. Meta will lease the full 168 MW capacity, with options to scale further. Delivery is expected within two years.

"Building India's first built-to-suit data centre for a global technology leader of Meta's scale demonstrates India's readiness to be at the forefront of the global AI revolution," Ambani said in a joint statement. Zuckerberg said the facility would help Meta "scale its AI infrastructure globally while deepening long-term investment in India's economy."

## The Infrastructure Details

The data centre will run entirely on renewable energy. Reliance will supply the power from its own renewable assets at the Jamnagar complex, and the facility will use desalinated seawater for cooling — both funded by Meta. The setup avoids dependence on the grid, a meaningful advantage in a country where industrial power reliability remains uneven.

Meta is separately contracting nearly 1 gigawatt of new renewable energy capacity in India through partnerships with CleanMax (837 MW of solar and wind) and Fourth Partner Energy (88 MW). These are among the largest clean energy commitments any single tech company has made in the country.

The Jamnagar site will also plug into Meta's Project Waterworth — the world's longest subsea cable system — through India's western submarine cable landing stations, ensuring low-latency connectivity for AI workloads that need to move data between continents.

## The Strategic Context

The deal lands at a moment when every major American tech company is racing to secure data centre capacity in India. Amazon, Microsoft, and Google have all announced or expanded hyperscale facilities in recent months. In February, Reliance committed approximately $110 billion and Adani outlined $100 billion in investments to position India as a global AI hub. The government has offered foreign companies a 20-year-plus tax break for using Indian data centres.

India's data centre market is projected to nearly double to $13.11 billion by 2034, according to consulting firm IMARC Group. The growth is driven by digitalisation, cloud adoption, and the explosion of AI workloads — but also by a geopolitical recalibration that is pushing companies to diversify infrastructure away from a handful of locations.

For Meta specifically, the deal extends a relationship that began with a $5.7 billion investment in Jio Platforms in 2020 and deepened last year with a joint venture to deploy Meta's Llama AI models for Indian enterprises. The Jamnagar facility moves that partnership from software into physical infrastructure — a far more capital-intensive and longer-term commitment.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For Indian tech professionals working at Meta in the US and Europe, the Jamnagar facility signals that India is no longer just a talent source — it is becoming part of the company's core AI infrastructure. That shift could open roles in India-based AI operations, data centre engineering, and Llama model deployment that did not previously exist at this scale.

For NRI investors, the deal underscores the thesis that India's digital infrastructure is a multi-decade growth story. Reliance Industries shares have outperformed the Nifty 50 this year partly on the strength of such partnerships, and the data centre buildout adds a new revenue stream to Jio Platforms ahead of its anticipated IPO.

The broader signal is unmistakable. The company that connects 3.3 billion people — and is betting its future on AI — has decided that it needs computing power inside India, built by an Indian company, powered by Indian renewable energy. The days when India was only a consumer of American platforms are ending. It is now part of the supply chain that makes them work.
